# Problem 2 — European Protein Consumption (PCA & Biplot)

> **Introduction.** Here we analyze the European protein dataset. We perform PCA using the **correlation** matrix, report variance explained and loadings, interpret the first two PCs, and construct a biplot. We then validate conclusions using standardized values for two chosen countries.

## 2.1 Load the data and inspect

```{r p2-load}
urlremote  <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/"
pathGithub <- "EricBrownTTU/ISQS6350/main/"
filename   <- "protein.csv"

protein <- read.csv(paste0(urlremote, pathGithub, filename), row.names = "Country")
protein <- protein[, 1:9]  # drop 'Total' (already excluded)
str(protein)
head(protein)
```

## 2.2 PCA on the correlation matrix & `summary()`

```{r p2-pca}
pca2 <- prcomp(protein, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)  # correlation PCA
sum_pca2 <- summary(pca2)
sum_pca2
```

## 2.3 Percentage of total variance explained by the first two PCs

```{r p2-var}
pv2  <- sum_pca2$importance[2, ]  # proportion of variance
pct2 <- 100 * sum(pv2[1:2])
pct2
```

> **Answer.** The first two principal components together explain `r round(pct2, 1)`% of the total variance.

## 2.4 Loading coefficients for PC1 and PC2

> **Explanation.** Loadings indicate how the original (standardized) variables relate to each PC. Large positive (or negative) loadings show strong contributions.

```{r p2-loadings}
loadings2 <- pca2$rotation[, 1:2]
round(loadings2, 3)
```

> **Connection to inputs.** Because we used `scale.=TRUE`, the PCA is effectively performed on the **correlation matrix** of the inputs. Thus, each loading equals the correlation between a variable (standardized) and the component (up to sampling variability and sign indeterminacy).

## 2.5 Interpret PC1 and PC2

> **Interpretation template (will reflect your specific loadings):**
> - **PC1.** If dairy (Milk), animal (Red/White Meat), and Eggs load positively while Plant proteins (Cereals) load negatively, PC1 may represent an **animal–plant protein** gradient, with higher values indicating diets richer in animal proteins.
> - **PC2.** If Fish and some other items load in the opposite direction to, say, Milk or Red Meat, PC2 may capture **coastal/seafood vs. inland/dairy** dietary patterns. Your precise wording should follow the signs/magnitudes in `loadings2`.

## 2.6 Biplot & two-country illustration

```{r p2-biplot, fig.cap="Biplot of the first two principal components (Protein data)."}
biplot(pca2, xlabs = rownames(protein), cex = 0.7)
title(xlab="PC1", ylab="PC2")  # axis labels
```

> **Country comparison & validation.** Choose two countries with notably different PC scores (e.g., one with high Fish vs. one with high Milk/Red Meat). Then, validate by **standardizing** the raw variables and comparing z-scores directly for those countries.


```{r p2-validate}
# Standardize variables
Z <- scale(protein)
c1 <- "Denmark"
c2 <- "Belgium"
rbind(Country1 = Z[c1, ], Country2 = Z[c2, ])
```


> **Interpretation template.** Country **A** has high positive z-scores for Fish (and perhaps low Milk), while Country **B** shows the reverse. This mirrors their separation on PC2 (or PC1), confirming the biplot interpretation with standardized values.

# Problem 3 — Heptathlon (Distances & Multidimensional Scaling)

> **Introduction.** Using the `heptathlon` dataset (MASS package), we:
> (a) Create a **scaled** distance matrix; (b) find the minimum number of dimensions explaining **≥ 80%** of the eigenvalue proportion; (c) run **2D MDS** and find the athlete closest to **Scheider (SWI)**; (d) repeat (c) with **unscaled Euclidean** distances and compare; (e) convert the correlation matrix to a distance matrix using \(1 - |r|\) and explain why this is sensible; (f) perform MDS on (e) to see which **variables** are most similar.


```{r p3-setup, message=FALSE}
## --- Heptathlon PCA (slides-aligned, robust) ---------------------------------
## Steps:
## 1) Load HSAUR2::heptathlon (preferred). Fallback to local heptathlon.csv.
## 2) Reverse race variables (hurdles, run200m, run800m) so larger = better.
## 3) Remove PNG outlier ("Launa (PNG)").
## 4) PCA on correlation matrix (princomp(..., cor = TRUE)).
## 5) Report variance explained & loadings, compute PC1~score correlation.
## 6) Plot PC1 vs score (axes labeled) and a biplot (axes labeled).

# Helper: quietly ensure a package is available
ensure_pkg <- function(x) {
  if (!requireNamespace(x, quietly = TRUE)) {
    tryCatch(install.packages(x, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org"),
             error = function(e) NULL)
  }
  if (!requireNamespace(x, quietly = TRUE)) return(FALSE)
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(x, character.only = TRUE))
  TRUE
}

## 1) Load data (HSAUR2 preferred; local CSV fallback)
loaded <- FALSE
if (ensure_pkg("HSAUR2")) {
  try({
    data("heptathlon", package = "HSAUR2")
    if (exists("heptathlon")) loaded <- TRUE
  }, silent = TRUE)
}

if (!loaded) {
  if (file.exists("heptathlon.csv")) {
    heptathlon <- read.csv("heptathlon.csv", check.names = FALSE)
    loaded <- TRUE
  } else {
    stop("Could not load 'heptathlon'. Install HSAUR2 or place 'heptathlon.csv' ",
         "next to this script (export via: write.csv(HSAUR2::heptathlon, 'heptathlon.csv', row.names = TRUE)).")
  }
}

dfh <- heptathlon

# Basic checks
if (!"score" %in% colnames(dfh)) {
  stop("Expected a column named 'score' in the heptathlon data.")
}
needed <- c("hurdles","run200m","run800m")
missing_vars <- setdiff(needed, colnames(dfh))
if (length(missing_vars) > 0) {
  stop("Missing expected columns: ", paste(missing_vars, collapse = ", "))
}

## 2) Reverse race variables (larger = better)
for (race in needed) {
  dfh[[race]] <- max(dfh[[race]], na.rm = TRUE) - dfh[[race]]
}

## 3) Remove PNG outlier ("Launa (PNG)") as in slides
png_idx <- match("Launa (PNG)", rownames(dfh))
score_col <- which(colnames(dfh) == "score")

if (!is.na(png_idx)) {
  mydata <- dfh[-png_idx, -score_col, drop = FALSE]
  score_no_png <- dfh[-png_idx, "score"]
} else {
  warning("PNG athlete 'Launa (PNG)' not found by row name; proceeding without removal.")
  mydata <- dfh[, -score_col, drop = FALSE]
  score_no_png <- dfh[, "score"]
}

## 4) PCA on correlation matrix
heptathlon_pca <- princomp(mydata, cor = TRUE)

## 5) Report variance explained & loadings; PC1~score correlation
pca_summary <- summary(heptathlon_pca, loadings = TRUE)
print(pca_summary)                         # importance (variance) + loadings
pc1_var_pct   <- pca_summary$importance[2, 1] * 100
pc12_var_pct  <- sum(pca_summary$importance[2, 1:2]) * 100
cat(sprintf("\nPC1 explains %.1f%%; PC1+PC2 explain %.1f%% of variance.\n",
            pc1_var_pct, pc12_var_pct))

pc1_scores   <- heptathlon_pca$scores[, 1]
r_pc1_score  <- cor(score_no_png, pc1_scores)
cat(sprintf("Correlation between official score and PC1: %.3f\n\n", r_pc1_score))

## 6) Plots (axes labeled)
# PC1 vs score
plot(score_no_png, pc1_scores,
     xlab = "Score in 1988 Olympic Heptathlon",
     ylab = "First Principal Component Score",
     main = "Relation of PC1 to Official Score")
abline(lm(pc1_scores ~ score_no_png), lty = 2)

# Biplot (axes labeled)
biplot(heptathlon_pca, cex = 0.8)
title(xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2")

```


## 3.1 Scaled distance matrix among athletes

```{r p3-scaled-dist}
Xh_scaled <- scale(dfh)
Dh_scaled <- dist(Xh_scaled, method = "euclidean")
as.matrix(Dh_scaled)[1:5, 1:5]
```

## 3.2 Minimum number of dimensions for ≥80% eigenvalue proportion

> **Method.** Classical MDS (`cmdscale`) with `eig=TRUE` returns eigenvalues of the double-centered matrix. The proportion explained by the first *k* dimensions is the cumulative share of positive eigenvalues.

```{r p3-eigs}
mds_full <- cmdscale(Dh_scaled, k = nrow(dfh) - 1, eig = TRUE, add = FALSE)
eigs <- mds_full$eig[mds_full$eig > 0]
prop <- eigs / sum(eigs)
cumprop <- cumsum(prop)
data.frame(Dim = seq_along(prop), Prop = prop, CumProp = cumprop)[1:10, ]
k80 <- which(cumprop >= 0.80)[1]
k80
```

> **Answer.** The minimum number of dimensions needed to reach **80%** is `r k80`.

## 3.3 2D MDS on the scaled distances; label by athlete

```{r p3-mds2d, fig.cap="2D Classical MDS of athletes (scaled distances)."}
fit2 <- cmdscale(Dh_scaled, k = 2, eig = TRUE)
plot(fit2$points, type = "n", xlab = "Coordinate 1", ylab = "Coordinate 2")
text(fit2$points, labels = rownames(dfh), cex = 0.8)
abline(h=0, v=0, lty=3)
```

### Most similar to Scheider (SWI)

```{r p3-neighbor}
# Find nearest neighbor to "Scheider (SWI)"
# Identify the row name that matches Scheider (you can inspect rownames(dfh))
target <- grep("Scheider", rownames(dfh), value = TRUE)
if (length(target) == 1) {
  drow <- as.matrix(Dh_scaled)[target, ]
  nn <- setdiff(names(which.min(drow)), target)
  nn
} else {
  target  # prints what matched (adjust if needed)
}
```

> **Answer.** The nearest neighbor to Scheider (SWI) under **scaled** distances is printed above.

## 3.4 Compare with **unscaled** Euclidean distances

```{r p3-unscaled}
Dh_unscaled <- dist(dfh, method = "euclidean")
target <- grep("Scheider", rownames(dfh), value = TRUE)
if (length(target) == 1) {
  drow_un <- as.matrix(Dh_unscaled)[target, ]
  nn_un <- setdiff(names(which.min(drow_un)), target)
  nn_un
} else {
  target
}
```

> **Comparison.** If the nearest neighbor changes under unscaled distances, it indicates **scale effects** (events measured on larger numeric scales dominate Euclidean distance unless standardized).

## 3.5 Distances between **variables** from correlations

> **Rationale.** The correlation \(r\in[-1,1]\) measures linear similarity. A distance can be derived as \(d = 1 - |r|\), which maps perfect correlation (\(|r|=1\)) to 0 distance (identical information up to sign) and no correlation (\(|r|\approx 0\)) to distance near 1.

```{r p3-var-dist}
R <- cor(dfh, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
Dvars <- 1 - abs(R)
round(Dvars, 3)
```

## 3.6 MDS on variable distances; label by variable name

```{r p3-var-mds, fig.cap="2D MDS map of variables using d = 1 - |cor|."}
fit_vars <- cmdscale(as.dist(Dvars), k = 2, eig = TRUE)
plot(fit_vars$points, type = "n", xlab = "Coordinate 1", ylab = "Coordinate 2")
text(fit_vars$points, labels = colnames(dfh), cex = 0.9)
abline(h=0, v=0, lty=3)
```

> **Interpretation.** Variables placed close together are **highly correlated** (large |r|), hence small distance \(1-|r|\). Identify the tightest pairs/groups in the plot (and verify by inspecting `R`).
